Everything's currently uncommitted on `main` (no branch, no commits yet), so below is the PR draft ready to use once it's on a branch. It's genuinely one large feature PR (~4,700 new lines: 2,628 Go, 1,378 JS, plus CSS/scripts, 6 new test files) since the whole GUI grew in one arc. I've written it in your voice, no em dashes.

---

**Title:**
`Add forgemark serve: a local web GUI with live push-race views, multi-forge comparison, and GitLab support`

**Branch:** `feat/web-gui-race` (suggested; nothing is committed yet)

---

## Body

```markdown
## What this does

Adds `forgemark serve`: a loopback web GUI over the same benchmark engine the
CLI drives, so you can configure a run in the browser, watch several forges
race live, and compare them fairly (every concurrency level starts at the same
instant on all targets). The headline is a **push race** view built for demos,
plus the full charts dashboard for analysis.

It also refactors the engine out of `cmd/forgemark` into `internal/bench` so
the CLI and the server are both thin frontends over one core, adds GitLab as a
first-class target, and reskins the UI to match entire.io.

## What's new

**Web GUI (`internal/server`, `forgemark serve`)**
- Multi-target comparison runs (up to 8), level-aligned, one active run at a
  time so load generators can't perturb each other's numbers.
- Live per-second stats streamed over SSE; a fresh load, a late join, and a
  reconnect are the same code path (replay from Last-Event-ID).
- Embedded single-page UI (no build step, vanilla ES modules): New run,
  Dashboard, Race, Runs, History.
- Binds loopback by default; mutating endpoints reject cross-origin requests.

**Race view (`#race/<id>`)**
- Three metrics you can switch live or deep-link: throughput (cumulative
  successful ops), latency (rolling p50, lower wins, bar length is relative
  speed), and reliability (successful ops / attempts).
- A methodology caption generated from the run's actual workload states exactly
  what is being measured, including that client-side round-trip is in every
  number. Exact ties are called a dead heat, never a false winner.

**Credentials from your CLIs, never pasted**
- A target can carry a `secret_source` (`gh` | `glab` | `entire`) and the
  server pulls the credential from your already-authenticated CLI at run start.
  The token never appears in a request body, a response, or the browser.
- `GET /api/local/suggest` discovers ready-to-run GitHub / GitLab / Entire
  targets from whichever CLIs you're logged into.

**GitLab support**
- Full parity with GitHub in the convenience layer. GitLab's git push needs a
  repository-scoped credential, which `glab auth token` does not always return,
  so the server uses glab's git-credential helper (username `oauth2` plus a
  repo-scoped password), queried for the target's host so self-managed GitLab
  works too.

**Scripts (`scripts/`)**
- `login.sh` authenticates the forge CLIs (glab optional).
- `compare-local.sh` starts a GitHub vs Entire comparison with zero token
  handling and auto-provisions the throwaway repos / mirror / native repo.
- `pushrace.sh` presets the 60s race workload and opens the race view.

**Design**
- Reskinned to entire.io's language: warm near-black surfaces, orange accent,
  mono eyebrow labels.
- New-run form reworked around a start-mode chooser (Compare my forges /
  Custom) with progressive disclosure: workload tuning and per-target advanced
  fields collapse behind disclosures, and an all-demo run skips the
  authorization checkbox since no real host is touched.

**Engine refactor**
- Benchmark engine moved from `cmd/forgemark/*` to `internal/bench`.
- New `internal/results` package owns the result-doc schema and read/write, so
  the CLI (legacy format 1) and server (format 2) share one parser.

## Architecture

One engine, two frontends. `bench.Runner.RunLevel` drives N agents pushing
real git over smart-HTTP through go-git. The CLI sweeps it and prints a table;
the server wraps it for multi-target comparison and streams an event log as
SSE. The frontend derives all state from that stream. Demo (`demo://`) targets
are a synthetic runner so the whole pipeline works offline.

## Safety

This is a load generator that can pull live tokens, so: loopback-only bind with
a warning when `-addr` is not loopback, cross-origin POSTs rejected, the
authorization confirmation preserved for any real target, and `Secret` carries
`json:"-"` so no marshal path can leak it.

## Testing

- `go test ./...` green across bench, results, server, and cmd.
- Verified end to end against real forges: GitHub and GitLab push races (branch
  strategy) and a clone-strategy demo run replayed correctly from History.
- Frontend driven headless across the chooser, both modes, and all three race
  metrics.

## Screenshots

- New-run chooser and Custom mode
- Push race (throughput / latency / reliability)
- Dashboard and History timeline replay

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
```

feat: forgemark serve, a local web GUI with live race views

Add `forgemark serve`: a loopback control panel over the same engine the CLI
drives. Configure a run in the browser, drive real git push/clone load against
one or more forges at once, and watch them side by side, level-aligned, with
per-second stats streamed over SSE.

Server (internal/server):
- RunManager enforces one active run at a time and starts every concurrency
  level simultaneously on all targets so the overlay is a fair comparison.
- A per-target collector implements bench.Sink and rolls 10s-window
  percentiles; an append-only event log fans out to SSE subscribers and
  replays from Last-Event-ID, so a fresh load, a late join, and a reconnect
  are one code path.
- demo:// targets are a synthetic runner so the whole pipeline works offline.
- Credentials are never pasted when you don't want them to be: a target can
  name a secret_source (gh | glab | entire) and the server pulls the token
  from your authenticated CLI at run start (GET /api/local/suggest discovers
  ready-to-run GitHub/GitLab/Entire targets). GitLab uses glab's
  git-credential helper, which returns a repository-scoped token even when
  glab's stored API token lacks that scope.
- Loopback-only bind with a warning when -addr isn't loopback, cross-origin
  POSTs rejected, and Target.Secret carries json:"-" so no marshal path can
  leak it.

UI (embedded vanilla-JS SPA, no build step):
- New run: a start-mode chooser (Compare my forges / Custom) with workload
  tuning and per-target advanced fields behind progressive disclosure; an
  all-demo run skips the authorization checkbox since no real host is touched.
- Dashboard: live throughput / latency-percentile / error charts (uPlot).
- Race: a demo-grade head-to-head with three metrics (throughput, latency,
  reliability) and a methodology caption built from the run's real workload.
- History: overlay any stored run's sweep curves and replay its timeline.
- Styled to entire.io's design language: warm-black surfaces, orange accent,
  mono eyebrow labels.

Two honest notes on the commit structure:

- **The engine and GUI commits are best reviewed together.** Commit 1 rewrites `main.go` into its final form, which wires the `serve` subcommand (`runServe`) that actually arrives with the server in commit 2. So commit 1 alone won't compile in isolation, even though the branch tip is fully green. If you want each commit independently buildable for `git bisect`, tell me and I'll do a quick reorder/fixup (it's a ~10-line shuffle of the serve dispatch).
- **Race, GitLab/credentials, and the redesign aren't separate commits** because they're interwoven in the same files (`runmgr.go`, `newrun.js`, `style.css`, `local.go`) that only ever existed in final form. Splitting them further would need hunk-level surgery rather than a clean file grouping, which tends to produce artificial, broken intermediate states. The PR draft I gave still describes them as distinct feature areas for the reviewer.

When you push, `gh` will print the compare URL; say the word and I'll open the PR with the draft title and body (I'd want your go-ahead since that's outward-facing).
Maybe we should never have built a web UI, maybe it should have always been the same concepts, but via TUI, which is closer to forgemark originally right?

Partly right, but "never" is too strong. The useful way to cut it: forgemark has two jobs, and they point at different interfaces.

**As an operator's instrument, your instinct is correct, and the strongest reason is one we spent a whole review pass papering over.** forgemark is meant to run close to the target, which in practice means a benchmarking box in the same region, reached over SSH. On that box a TUI is native: `ssh in, run forgemark, watch`. The web UI instead means port-forwarding a loopback socket, and worse, it's an HTTP server sitting on a machine holding live forge tokens. Every bit of the `secret_source` indirection, the loopback-origin CSRF guard, the `json:"-"` on the secret, the "is this bound to a real interface" warning, all of that exists to contain a threat model a local TUI process simply doesn't have. It can read `gh auth token` or the env directly and never expose a port. For an open-source load generator, "no network surface, single Go binary, no JS/CSS/SSE to audit" is a real simplicity and safety win, and it keeps the whole project in one language for contributors.

**As a demo artifact, the web UI earns its place.** The race is a presentation you put on a screen for an audience, sometimes a non-technical one. Big animated counters, a podium, latency percentile curves with a legend: pixels beat a terminal there. You are Field CTO; "watch Entire outrun GitHub 20x, live" is a sales moment, and the browser tells that story more legibly than sparklines.

**The good news: almost nothing is wasted.** The refactor put the real work in `internal/bench`, and both the CLI and `serve` are thin frontends over it. A TUI is just a third frontend over the same engine. The only web-specific sunk cost is the server package and the static assets.

What I'd actually do: don't rip out the web UI right before launch, that's churn for no gain. Ship it, but frame `serve`/race explicitly as the demo surface, and add a `forgemark tui` (Bubble Tea over the existing engine) as the primary interactive path for real runs. That gives you the SSH-native, credential-safe daily driver and keeps the shareable demo.

Want me to prototype the TUI over the current engine so you can compare them side by side before deciding what leads?
Perfect. Then, we should keep the web as a demo surface only and keep the core of forgemark largely pure to the original state. Is that possible? This way then we can do a TUI for the same

content.text:
Yes, and the good news is it is already true by every measure that matters. The verification above proves it:

**The dependency graph is already clean:**
```
internal/bench   (engine: go-git + stdlib + singleflight; zero web, zero doc-format deps)
  ├── cmd/forgemark        the original CLI, thin over the engine
  ├── internal/server      the web demo, reached only by cmd/forgemark/serve.go
  └── internal/results     shared doc I/O (the engine doesn't even import it)
```

- The engine's `net/http` and `encoding/json` are git transport and the entiredb OAuth exchange. Those were in pre-web forgemark. No HTTP server, no `embed`, no JSON wire shapes for a browser leaked in.
- Exactly one file (`serve.go`) touches the server package. The web is a single amputatable limb.
- The CLI flag surface is the original set (`remote`, `token-file`, `repos`, `strategy`, `concurrency`, ...) plus the entiredb flags that predate the web work. Nothing web-specific bent the CLI.

**The seam that makes "same core, many frontends" work is already there:** `bench.Sink`. The web collector implements it to get live samples; a TUI implements the same interface for its live view. Building the TUI needs zero engine changes. That is the whole payoff of the refactor.

**Nothing needs reverting to be "pure to original."** The only two engine-side changes the web era introduced are the exported `Sink`/`Sample` (frontend-agnostic, the TUI wants it too) and the CLI writing through `internal/results` instead of hand-rolled JSON (behavior-identical, still format-1). Both are improvements, not web contamination.

So the one real decision is how loud the "demo only" boundary should be:

- **Keep `serve` as a subcommand** of the one binary (current). Core stays pure, web runs only if you type `forgemark serve`. Recommended: it is discoverable, and `net/http` is already a transitive dep via go-git, so splitting would not even shrink the core's surface.
- **Split the web into its own binary** (`cmd/forgemark-demo`). A louder quarantine, at the cost of a second install target. Only worth it if you want the statement.

I would keep it as a subcommand and move on. Want me to prototype `forgemark tui` (Bubble Tea over the existing engine and its `Sink`) now, so you can drive a real run in the terminal and compare it head to head with the web race before you lock the direction?

Reviewed PR #11 against its diff (local checkout is exactly at the PR head). It's a clean extraction; the substantive review is on the four genuinely-new/changed files, not the renames.

## Overview

Lifts the engine out of `package main` into `internal/bench` (with a frontend-agnostic `Sink`) and `internal/results`, leaving `cmd/forgemark` a thin flag layer. Behavior-preserving by design. Builds, vets, and tests pass.

## What's solid

- **The `Sink` seam is the right abstraction.** `NewRunner(..., sink)` with the CLI passing `nil` keeps the engine frontend-agnostic without special-casing. This is the whole point of the refactor and it lands cleanly.
- **`internal/bench` has no outward dependencies** — no results package, no server, no HTTP server. The one purity boundary that matters is intact.
- **`NewRunner` orders its guards safely**: `w.Validate()` runs before `slices.Max(w.Concurrency)`, and Validate rejects empty concurrency, so the max can't panic.
- **Security is preserved**: `Target.Secret` carries `json:"-"`, `readSecret` keeps the token off argv, no secret is logged.
- **`results` test coverage is good**: round-trip, legacy normalization, path-traversal rejection, List skip/sort/missing-dir.

## Findings (all low severity)

- **The "byte-compatible" result output claim is slightly wrong** (`writeResults`, main.go:253). The old CLI marshaled a `map[string]any`, which Go emits with **alphabetically sorted keys**; the new code marshals a `results.Doc` struct, emitted in **field-declaration order**. Same fields, same values, parses identically through `Load`, but the serialized key order changed, so it is *semantically* compatible, not byte-identical. Also `Levels` has `json:"levels,omitempty"`, so a run cancelled before any level completes now omits the key where the old code wrote `"levels":null`. Neither breaks any parser, but the PR body should say "format-compatible" rather than imply identical bytes.

`high effort → 3+5 angles × 6 candidates → 1-vote verify (recall-biased) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** via the Agent tool. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates bypass the verify step and are the
dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Verify (1-vote, recall-biased)

Dedup near-duplicates (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). For
each remaining candidate, run **one verifier** via the Agent tool:
give it the diff, the relevant file(s), and the candidate; it returns exactly
one of **CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE / REFUTED**.

**PLAUSIBLE by default** — do not refute a candidate for being "speculative" or
"depends on runtime state" when the state is realistic: concurrency races,
nil/undefined on a rare-but-reachable path (error handler, cold cache, missing
optional field), falsy-zero treated as missing, off-by-one on a boundary the
code does not exclude, retry storms / partial failures, regex/allowlist that
lost an anchor. These are PLAUSIBLE.

**REFUTED** only when constructible from the code: factually wrong (quote the
actual line); provably impossible (type/constant/invariant — show it); already
handled in this diff (cite the guard); or pure style with no observable effect.

Keep **CONFIRMED and PLAUSIBLE**. Drop REFUTED.

## Output

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives verification, return `[]`.

So rather than build a plan on a guessed definition, here's my **working model** of an Entire Runner, then a compact idea cut. Correct the model and I'll harden the plan around it.

**My working model of an Entire Runner:** a managed, triggered, repeatable execution unit that runs a defined job close to the repo/data (Entire already mirrors repos regionally "for maximum agent throughput"), emits results Entire records as sessions/checkpoints, and can be fronted by a Gate (a pass/fail check) and sequenced in a Trail (a workflow). Essentially CI runners, but native to Entire's agent-SDLC and regional footprint.

**Why forgemark fits this unusually well:** forgemark's own README says the one thing you must do for valid numbers is *run the generator close to the target, same region*. Today that means manually SSHing to a box in-region. Entire already has regional clusters (us/eu/au/in) and mirrors. A forgemark Runner is the missing piece that makes "benchmark the forge from where the agents actually are" a one-click, repeatable thing.

**The runner taxonomy I'd propose, ranked:**

1. **Regional runner** (the headline). Entire schedules forgemark into a cluster's region and benchmarks that cluster from-region, so numbers aren't RTT-dominated by a laptop. This is the differentiated one and it directly exploits Entire's regional + mirror infrastructure. Heaviest to build (needs the in-region execution + phone-home path).

2. **Scheduled canary runner.** Runs a benchmark suite on a cron, stores each run as an Entire session/checkpoint, tracks throughput/latency as a trend, and flags regressions. Turns forgemark from a one-shot into continuous forge-health monitoring.

3. **CI / Gate runner.** Runs a benchmark as a PR or deploy check and gates on thresholds (p95 ceiling, ops/s floor), exit-code + annotation. This is a "Gate" in your terms, and it's the smallest, most concrete first step. Notably, **open PR #6 already adds threshold flags for CI regression gating** — the gating primitive is being built, so a runner just wraps it.

4. **Matrix runner.** Headless, distributed version of the race: same workload across forges × regions × strategies, aggregated into one comparison. The race view becomes its report.

**How it lands architecturally** (no engine rework): keep `internal/bench` (engine) and `internal/results` (doc format). A "runner" is just another headless driver over the engine plus a **result sink** — local JSON today, plus new sinks for Entire (store via `entire api`) and CI (annotation + threshold exit code). Trail = a named suite of runs; Gate = a threshold check over a run's results.

**My recommendation on sequencing:** CI/Gate first as the MVP (leverages PR #6, smallest, immediately useful), then scheduled canary (adds trend/regression + Entire storage), then the regional runner as the strategic headline once the managed-execution path exists.

Two things I need from you before I write the full plan:

1. **Correct my Runner model** — especially how Runners relate to Trails and Gates, and whether a Runner is Entire-managed compute (my assumption) or a client-side concept.
2. **Which end to start from** — the strategic headline (regional, managed) or the pragmatic MVP (CI/Gate on top of PR #6)?

content.text:
Found the real thing, and it sharpens the plan a lot. Here's what an Entire Runner actually is, then the forgemark plan grounded in it.

## What a Runner is (from `.entire/runners/*.json` in the cli and git-sync repos)

A Runner is a declarative job file: `scope: trail` (a branch's changes vs its base), triggered on `push`/`api`, executed in a sandbox with a scoped repo token, producing a typed `output`. The `entire runner setup/tune` command scaffolds them (hidden "during maturation", which is why it's absent from the public docs). The stock set is seven: `summary`, `review`, `review-focus`, `risk`, `security`, `confidence`, `drift`.

Three output types matter:
- **`trail_summary`** — markdown (the Problem/Solution summary).
- **`code_review_comments`** — inline findings with severity/confidence/location.
- **`trail_monitor`** — a scored metric: `{key, label, value_type: percent, polarity: lower_is_better|higher_is_better}`, value 0-100. This is the gateable signal (Risk, Security, Drift are all monitors).

## The key insight

**All seven stock runners are `prompt_runner`s: an LLM reads a diff and judges it.** None of them *run* anything. forgemark would be the first **execution-based runner that emits measured, empirical signals** into the exact same Trail machinery. A forgemark benchmark maps perfectly onto `trail_monitor`: throughput (higher_is_better), p95 latency (lower_is_better), error/CAS rate (lower_is_better). So instead of an LLM guessing whether a change is risky, forgemark tells the Trail what the change actually did to forge performance, and it shows up next to Risk and Security and can back a Gate.

## The forgemark runner set I'd propose

Concrete `.entire/runners/*.json`, each a benchmark that runs on push and emits a monitor:

| Runner | Output | Metric | Polarity |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trail-throughput` | trail_monitor | push ops/s (branch sweep) | higher_is_better |
| `trail-latency` | trail_monitor | p95 ms | lower_is_better |
| `trail-forge-errors` | trail_monitor | error + CAS rate | lower_is_better |
| `trail-perf` | trail_summary | the race table rendered as markdown | — |

That's the demo race, but headless, per-branch, and gateable.

## The two build layers

**1. Definitions + a forgemark output adapter (small, mostly in this repo).** The runners are JSON, but forgemark needs a machine-readable *monitor* mode: reduce a `results.Doc` to the runner's `{"value": <n>, "rationale": "..."}` last-JSON-line contract. A `forgemark report --emit monitor` (or a `--format entire`) over the existing engine + `internal/results`. Cheap, and it's the seam everything else hangs off.

**2. The runtime (the real work, needs Entire).** Every stock runner uses the read-only `claude` sandbox. forgemark is different: it needs the forgemark binary, **network egress to the target forge**, and ideally **regional placement** (forgemark's whole methodology caveat is "run close to the target"). That's a new runner profile, and it's exactly where Entire's regional clusters + mirrors are the differentiator. Two ways to get the `runtime.kind`:
- Reuse `prompt_runner` as an MVP: a runner whose prompt is "run `forgemark ...`, emit the result JSON as the last line" (works with today's adapter, if the sandbox allows egress).
- A proper non-prompt kind. I saw hints of `agent_runner`, `trail_runner`, and one `script_runner` reference but no `command_runner`/`exec_runner`, so a measured/exec runner kind looks like a genuine gap forgemark would be the first real user of.

## Sequencing

1. **forgemark monitor-output mode** — the adapter (this repo, no Entire dependency).
2. **CI/Gate proof** — wire it into GitHub Actions on top of open PR #6's threshold flags: forgemark runs, emits the monitor value, gates the PR. Proves the signal with zero new Entire infra.
3. **Native Entire runner** — the regional, egress-capable runtime that runs forgemark in-region and posts monitors to the Trail. The strategic headline.

## What I need from you

1. Does a Gate already threshold a `trail_monitor` (so `throughput < X` fails a Trail), or is Gate still to build? That decides whether forgemark just emits and rides existing gating, or we build the gate too.
2. Is there an exec/command/`script_runner` runtime, or would forgemark be the case that justifies one? This is the biggest scope fork.
3. Sandbox reality: can a runner sandbox make outbound git connections and be pinned to a region? That's the gating constraint on the native runner.

Want me to draft the four runner JSON files and the `forgemark report --emit monitor` adapter as a concrete first PR (layer 1), so there's something real to run in CI while the runtime questions get answered?

## What this does

Adds `forgemark serve`: a loopback web GUI over the same engine the CLI drives,
framed as the demo surface (the CLI stays the operator's tool). Configure a run
in the browser, drive real git push/clone load against one or more forges at
once, and watch them race live. Builds on the merged engine refactor (#11); the
CLI and the trail runners on `main` are untouched.

## What's new

**`forgemark serve` (internal/server)**
- Multi-target comparison runs, one active at a time, every concurrency level
  started simultaneously so the overlay is a fair comparison.
- A per-target collector implements `bench.Sink` and rolls 10s-window
  percentiles; an append-only event log fans out over SSE and replays from
  `Last-Event-ID`, so a fresh load, a late join, and a reconnect are one path.
- `demo://` targets are a synthetic runner so the whole pipeline works offline.

**Live race view (`#race/<id>`)**
- A head-to-head with three metrics (throughput, latency, reliability),
  switchable live and deep-linkable, plus a methodology caption generated from
  the run's actual workload. Exact ties are called a dead heat.

**Credentials from your CLIs, never pasted**
- A target names a `secret_source` (`gh` | `glab` | `entire`) and the server
  pulls the credential from your authenticated CLI at run start, so the browser
  never holds a token. `GET /api/local/suggest` prefills GitHub / GitLab /
  Entire targets. GitLab goes through glab's git-credential helper (a
  repository-scoped token even when glab's API token isn't).

**Scripts** — `login.sh`, `compare-local.sh` (zero token handling,
auto-provisions the throwaway repos / mirror / native repo), `pushrace.sh`.

**Design** — the New-run form is a start-mode chooser with progressive
disclosure; the whole UI is styled to entire.io's warm-black + orange language.

## Safety

It's a load generator that can pull live tokens: loopback-only bind with a
warning when `-addr` isn't loopback, cross-origin POSTs rejected, and
`Target.Secret` carries `json:"-"` so no marshal path can leak it.

## Testing

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` all green; JS and scripts
  syntax-checked; live smoke of `serve` plus GitHub / GitLab / Entire runs.
- The final commit applies a full `/code-review` pass over this branch
  (latency-gate blanking, an allDemo/blank-target mismatch, secret-exec ordering
  before the active-run check, `serve -h` exit code, a script cluster wiring
  bug, and CSS/dead-state cleanups), each with a test or live check.

Traced it to the source. Here's the answer, and it's more specific than "not wired."

**Where the wiring comes from:** the Entire **GitHub App**. `entire enable` posts to `/api/v1/cli/enable`, which records the repo and reports whether the App can reach it (returning an `InstallURL` to the App install page when it can't). Push events delivered through that App drive the trail engine, which reads the per-repo `.entire/runners/*.json` and runs each one over a trail (a branch-vs-base diff). For forgemark this wiring **is present and healthy**: the mirror record shows `status: ready`, `installationId: 104585035`, cell `aws-us-east-2`, and the trail engine already created the trail for your PR.

**So it's not the App and not the runner files. The actual failure is one step downstream:** the trail (`#2`, id `01KYKH3VQNRHF5TDKWR8RM9MDE`) is stuck at `phase: building` with **`baseSha: null` and `mergeBaseSha: null`**. Every runner prompt diffs `origin/{{base_branch}}...HEAD`, so with no resolved base the engine has no diff to hand them. Nothing runs, which is exactly what you see: `monitors: []`, zero review comments, no runner executions. The head SHA (`d89139e`) is correct; only the base against `main` never resolved.

**Why the base is null:** the trail engine couldn't compute the merge-base of your head against `main` on the Entire side. That's a base/mirror resolution problem, not a repo problem. Most likely the mirror's `main` history needed to compute the merge-base isn't fully ingested (your branch was rebased onto the just-merged `d15ceaf`, so the engine needs the mirror to have `main` at `d15ceaf` to find the base). The trail sitting in `building` for hours with a null base is the tell.

**What I'd do to confirm and unstick it:**

11	// windowSecs is the rolling-percentile window: latency percentiles in a bucket
12	// event are computed over the OK samples of the last windowSecs seconds, so a
13	// single quiet second doesn't blank the lines while spikes still show quickly.
14	const windowSecs = 10
15	
16	// collector is the live aggregator for one target of one run. It implements
17	// bench.Sink: agents call OnSample concurrently mid-measurement, so it does
18	// only counter increments and one append under its mutex. Once per second the
19	// run's ticker calls snapshot, which swaps the current bucket out and computes
20	// rolling percentiles (an exact sort over the window — a few thousand floats,
21	// ~100µs, nothing at benchmark sample rates).
22	type collector struct {
23		mu        sync.Mutex
24		cur       bucket
25		ring      [windowSecs][]float64 // push OK latencies, one slot per elapsed second
26		cloneRing [windowSecs][]float64
27		pos       int
28	}
29	
30	// bucket accumulates one second of samples.
31	type bucket struct {
32		ok, cas, errs     int
33		cloneOK, cloneErr int
34		lat               []float64 // OK push latencies (ms)
35		cloneLat          []float64 // OK clone latencies (ms)
36	}
37	
38	// BucketStats is one target's slice of a per-second bucket event. Push and
39	// clone ops are reported separately, mirroring LevelResult; the UI picks the
40	// primary series from the workload strategy. Attempt totals are derivable
41	// (ok+cas+err, clone_ok+clone_err), so they aren't carried on the wire.
42	type BucketStats struct {
43		OK  int `json:"ok"`
44		CAS int `json:"cas"`
45		Err int `json:"err"`
46		// Rolling percentiles over the last windowSecs seconds of OK pushes.
47		P50 float64 `json:"p50_ms"`
48		P95 float64 `json:"p95_ms"`
49		P99 float64 `json:"p99_ms"`
50	
51		CloneOK  int     `json:"clone_ok,omitempty"`
52		CloneErr int     `json:"clone_err,omitempty"`
53		CloneP50 float64 `json:"clone_p50_ms,omitempty"`
54		CloneP95 float64 `json:"clone_p95_ms,omitempty"`
55		CloneP99 float64 `json:"clone_p99_ms,omitempty"`
56	}
57	
58	func (c *collector) OnSample(s bench.Sample) {
59		ms := float64(s.Dur) / float64(time.Millisecond)
60		c.mu.Lock()
61		defer c.mu.Unlock()
62		if s.Op == bench.OpClone {
63			switch s.Res {
64			case bench.OutcomeOK:
65				c.cur.cloneOK++
66				c.cur.cloneLat = append(c.cur.cloneLat, ms)
67			default:
68				c.cur.cloneErr++
69			}
70			return
71		}
72		switch s.Res {
73		case bench.OutcomeOK:
74			c.cur.ok++
75			c.cur.lat = append(c.cur.lat, ms)
76		case bench.OutcomeCAS:
77			c.cur.cas++
78		default:
79			c.cur.errs++
80		}
81	}
82	
83	// snapshot closes out the current second: it returns its counters and the
84	// rolling percentiles over the updated window.
85	func (c *collector) snapshot() BucketStats {
86		c.mu.Lock()
87		b := c.cur
88		c.cur = bucket{}
89		c.ring[c.pos] = b.lat
90		c.cloneRing[c.pos] = b.cloneLat
91		c.pos = (c.pos + 1) % windowSecs
92		var lat, cloneLat []float64
93		for i := range c.ring {
94			lat = append(lat, c.ring[i]...)
95			cloneLat = append(cloneLat, c.cloneRing[i]...)
96		}
97		c.mu.Unlock()
98	
99		st := BucketStats{
100			OK: b.ok, CAS: b.cas, Err: b.errs,
101			CloneOK: b.cloneOK, CloneErr: b.cloneErr,
102		}
103		if len(lat) > 0 {
104			sort.Float64s(lat)
105			st.P50 = bench.Percentile(lat, 50)
106			st.P95 = bench.Percentile(lat, 95)
107			st.P99 = bench.Percentile(lat, 99)
108		}
109		if len(cloneLat) > 0 {
110			sort.Float64s(cloneLat)
111			st.CloneP50 = bench.Percentile(cloneLat, 50)
112			st.CloneP95 = bench.Percentile(cloneLat, 95)
113			st.CloneP99 = bench.Percentile(cloneLat, 99)
114		}
115		return st
116	}
117	
118	// reset clears the bucket and the rolling window. Called at each level start
119	// so percentiles never bleed across concurrency levels.
120	func (c *collector) reset() {
121		c.mu.Lock()
122		defer c.mu.Unlock()
123		c.cur = bucket{}
124		c.ring = [windowSecs][]float64{}
125		c.cloneRing = [windowSecs][]float64{}

content.text:
All six trail review findings are fixed, pushed, and CI is green (`30261ae`: lint pass, test pass).

**High severity (security):**
- **Origin check** (`server.go`): now requires the Origin to match the server's own host:port, not just a loopback hostname. Closes the cross-port CSRF where another local dev server could drive runs / pull CLI credentials via a simple no-preflight POST.
- **secret_source audience** (`runmgr.go` + `local.go`): each source is pinned to its issuer before the credential is ever materialized — `gh`→github.com, `glab`→gitlab.com, `entire`→`*.entire.io` for remote/token_url/jurisdiction. A spec can no longer leak the GitHub token to an attacker's remote or POST the Entire subject token to an arbitrary token_url.

**Medium (correctness/perf):**
- **Collector mutex** (`collector.go`): the rolling-window concat now happens after unlocking (slice headers copied under lock), so the per-second snapshot stops blocking concurrent `OnSample` and depressing measured throughput.
- **Warm-up exclusion** (`collector.go`): warm-up samples are dropped, so live counts/percentiles/persisted series match the authoritative level result.
- **Level-transition race** (`runmgr.go`): collectors reset and level index advance atomically under `r.mu`, and `emitBucket` holds that lock across its snapshot, so a tick can't attribute the previous level's samples to the new index.
- **Real start barrier** (`bench.StartBarrier` + `RunLevel`): all targets build agents, then release together, so setup-time skew no longer breaks the level-aligned comparison. It's failure-tolerant (a target that dies in setup still arrives, so the coordinator can't hang).

Verified with `go test -race` (no data races), `golangci-lint` (0 issues), and a live 2-target × 2-level demo run that completed cleanly with sensible scaling.

Two judgment calls worth flagging:
- The warm-up fix means the live/replay charts no longer plot the warm-up ramp (the shaded band becomes an empty lead-in). That's the consistent, honest behavior the finding asked for; if you'd rather keep the ramp visible I can switch to reset-at-boundary instead.
- I pinned the CLI-sourced credential to public hosts (github.com/gitlab.com/*.entire.io). Self-hosted GHES/GitLab/Entire via `secret_source` will now be rejected — those should paste a token instead. Easy to relax to a configurable allowlist if you want self-hosted convenience.

The no-op commit `bbf117a` from the trail-debugging is still in the branch history; say the word and I'll drop it before merge.

High

Comparing Origin only to Host still accepts DNS rebinding: after evil.example:8377 rebinds to loopback, both headers remain evil.example:8377, allowing the hostile page to invoke CLI-sourced credentials and remote writes. Validate the request host against the configured loopback listener or an explicit allowlist, then require Origin to match that trusted host.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/static/js/views/newrun.js:255
14m ago

The custom-target path places the pasted credential in spec.targets[*].secret, so every such run serializes the token into an HTTP request; with the supported non-loopback -addr, it is also transmitted over cleartext HTTP. Keep credentials server-side via a source/file/opaque handle and never include the secret in JSON.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/runmgr.go:291
11h ago

secret_source is resolved and attached to any caller-supplied remote or token URL without validating its audience. For example, pairing "gh" with an attacker-controlled remote sends the GitHub token as Basic Auth, while an Entire token can be POSTed to an arbitrary token_url; reject source/target mismatches and pin exchange endpoints before materializing credentials.

Medium
AI
Trail Review
internal/server/runmgr.go:493
14m ago

Stopping the ticker without a final snapshot discards every sample collected since its last tick; the next level's reset similarly drops each level's partial final bucket. Live/persisted series and race totals therefore omit up to one second per level—and all samples for sub-second levels—despite the authoritative LevelResult containing them; flush collectors after each RunLevel before reset or shutdown.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/server.go:66
14m ago

Server cancellation shuts down HTTP but never cancels or waits for the active run, whose context was created from context.Background(). Embedded callers can return while remote load continues, while the CLI can exit before result persistence and session-ref cleanup; cancel the manager's active run and wait for its coordinator before returning.

Trail Review

11h ago

bench.Sink explicitly receives warm-up samples, but this collector records them unconditionally. Live charts, race totals/reliability, and persisted series therefore include warm-up even though the authoritative level result excludes it; filter by Sample.Offset or reset precisely at the warm-up boundary.

All six items from this trail review are resolved, pushed, and CI is green (`e0b21a1`: lint pass, test pass).

**The four new findings (fixed this round):**
- **DNS rebinding** (`server.go`) — my previous Origin==Host check didn't stop rebinding, since a rebound `evil.example:8377` keeps that value in both headers. Now, on a loopback bind, the request Host must be a loopback literal, which a rebinding attack can't forge; Origin==Host stays on top. Verified live: spoofed `Host: evil.example` → 403, normal loopback run works.
- **Pasted secret over cleartext** (`server.go`) — a pasted token in the request body would cross the LAN in cleartext on a non-loopback `-addr`. Now refused there (must use `secret_source`); loopback paste is unchanged. Unit-tested.
- **Dropped tail bucket** (`runmgr.go`) — the 1s ticker dropped each level's final partial second (and all of a sub-second level). Now flushed via `emitBucket` after each level finishes. Verified: a ~3s run persisted 4 series points.
- **Shutdown vs active run** (`server.go`/`runmgr.go`) — the run's context was `Background`-derived, so shutdown left load running and results unwritten. Now shutdown cancels the active run and waits (bounded) for it to persist. Verified: SIGTERM mid-run wrote a `cancelled` doc with its series.

**The two carryovers** (secret_source audience, warm-up exclusion) were already fixed in the prior round — I confirmed both are present in the code, so they should clear once the review re-runs against `e0b21a1`.

All verified with `go test -race` (no data races on the concurrency-sensitive changes), `golangci-lint` clean, and live smoke.

Two judgment calls I want to be explicit about, since a stricter reading of the findings would go further:
- **Pasted secrets** — I kept loopback paste (it's on-machine, in-memory, never persisted or returned) and only blocked the cleartext-LAN path. The finding's ideal is "never serialize a secret into JSON," which would mean removing the paste option entirely and forcing `secret_source`/file. That's a product call — say the word and I'll drop paste.
- **`secret_source` host pinning** — still restricted to the public hosts (github.com/gitlab.com/*.entire.io), so self-hosted forges via a CLI source are rejected (paste on loopback instead). Easy to widen to a configurable allowlist if you want self-hosted convenience.

The trail-debugging no-op commit `bbf117a` is still in the branch history; I can drop it before merge whenever you like.

The custom-target path places the pasted credential in spec.targets[*].secret, so every such run serializes the token into an HTTP request; with the supported non-loopback -addr, it is also transmitted over cleartext HTTP. Done. Both CI checks (lint 30s, test 43s) pass on `feat/web-demo`.

## Round 3 trail-review findings, resolved

**`newrun.js:255` (High) — pasted credential serialized into request JSON.** Fixed with the source-only approach you picked. The web form no longer has a free-text credential field at all. Each non-demo target now names a credential source (`gh` / `glab` / `entire` CLI login) via a dropdown, and the server pulls the token locally at run start. No secret ever gets serialized into the browser request. Demo targets show "none needed (demo target)". Arbitrary forges go through the CLI's `-token-file`. Screenshot confirmed the rendered form: dropdown only, no token box.

**`runmgr.go:493` (Medium) — tail bucket dropped.** This was already fixed in an earlier round (`r.emitBucket()` flushes the tail after `lwg.Wait()`). It re-appeared as a finding only because the trail is stuck server-side (`baseSha: null`, phase never left `building`), so the reviewer is diffing against a stale/empty base and re-surfacing carryovers. No code action needed.

Verification before commit: `gofmt` clean, `go build ./...` clean, all four packages' tests pass, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `node --check` on newrun.js OK.

Commit `96885f9` pushed. The server keeps accepting a secret via the raw API (CLI/curl parity), still guarded by the non-loopback paste rejection, so nothing regresses for the CLI path.

One loose end still open from before: the no-op commit `bbf117a` is sitting in the `feat/web-demo` history. Want me to drop it before this merges, or leave it?

Findings

High
AI
Trail Review
internal/server/server.go:92
2h ago

For a non-loopback bind this disables the Host restriction, while requests without an Origin are accepted, so any reachable client can start/cancel runs and invoke secret_source resolution using the operator's gh/glab/Entire credentials against attacker-selected repositories. Require authentication for exposed binds, or refuse CLI credential sources and mutating APIs unless the server is loopback-only.

AI
Trail Review
scripts/compare-local.sh:106
2h ago

The quoted error is embedded inside double quotes and then evaluated, so command substitutions in a crafted /api/local/suggest error still execute (for example $(command)). Avoid eval entirely or pass parsed values through a non-evaluated channel rather than generating shell source.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/local.go:82
2h ago

Audience validation discards the URL scheme, so secret_source accepts targets such as http://github.com and http://*.entire.io; the locally obtained token is then sent over cleartext HTTP. Require HTTPS (and reject URL userinfo) for every CLI-sourced remote, token URL, and jurisdiction endpoint.

Medium
AI
Trail Review
internal/server/runmgr.go:505
2h ago

This flush emits the level's final fractional bucket as a raw count, but consumers label every bucket as ops/s or failures/s; ticker phase also makes the first post-warmup bucket fractional. Persist and expose each bucket's actual elapsed duration and normalize rates, or align bucket boundaries to the measured window.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/static/js/views/newrun.js:225
2h ago

Malformed numeric input produces NaN, which JSON.stringify converts to null; the server then treats that field as absent and silently applies defaults (for example an invalid duration becomes 60 seconds). Validate every numeric field as finite and, where applicable, integral before starting the run instead of silently launching a different workload.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/collector.go:61
2h ago

Every measured agent synchronously acquires the same collector mutex and may grow a latency slice while holding it. Since OnSample runs between operations, contention delays the next Git operation and depresses web throughput relative to the sink-free CLI; use sharded/atomic collection or a non-blocking observation path.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/server.go:42
2h ago

Only mutating routes receive the DNS-rebinding Host check; after rebinding an attacker-controlled origin to loopback, same-origin JavaScript can read /api/runs, run events, and history through Host: evil.example. Apply the loopback Host/origin guard to the read API routes as well, particularly run status and SSE.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/server.go:68
2h ago

Server shutdown waits only 10 seconds for the run, but session agents may synchronously perform ref cleanup using independent 30-second contexts. ListenAndServe can therefore return while cleanup/load is still active, or the CLI can exit before ephemeral refs are deleted; shutdown must wait for coordinator completion or make cleanup obey a sufficiently bounded shared shutdown context.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/runmgr.go:474
2h ago

level_start.at is emitted before every target builds its agents and reaches the barrier, while the measured timer starts only after the barrier releases. Setup delays therefore make the UI countdown and warm-up shading start early; emit the event immediately before firing the barrier or publish the actual measured start time.

211	// start validates a request and launches its coordinator. It returns
212	// user-facing warnings (e.g. the github.com abuse note) alongside the run.
213	func (m *RunManager) start(req startRequest) (*Run, []string, error) {
214		if !req.ConfirmAuthorized {
215			return nil, nil, errors.New("confirm_authorized must be true: only benchmark infrastructure you own or are explicitly authorized to load-test")
216		}
217		if len(req.Targets) == 0 {
218			return nil, nil, errors.New("at least one target is required")
219		}
220		if len(req.Targets) > maxTargets {
221			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("at most %d targets per run", maxTargets)
222		}
223	
224		ws := req.Workload.withDefaults()
225		runID := bench.NewRunID()
226		bw := ws.toWorkload(runID)
227		if err := bw.Validate(); err != nil {
228			return nil, nil, err
229		}
230	
231		var warnings []string
232		targets := make([]*targetState, len(req.Targets))
233		for i, ts := range req.Targets {
234			bt := ts.toTarget()
235			name := ts.Name
236			if name == "" {
237				name = defaultTargetName(bt.Remote, i)
238			}
239			if ts.SecretSource != "" && ts.Secret != "" {
240				return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("target %s: pass secret or secret_source, not both", name)
241			}
242			// Pin each CLI-sourced credential to its issuer's audience before it is
243			// ever materialized: otherwise a spec could pair "gh" with an attacker's
244			// remote (leaking the GitHub token as Basic Auth) or "entire" with an
245			// arbitrary token_url (leaking the subject token to the exchange). A
246			// self-hosted forge should paste a token instead of naming a CLI source.
247			if ts.SecretSource != "" {
248				if err := validateSecretAudience(ts.SecretSource, bt.Remote, bt.TokenURL, bt.Jurisdiction); err != nil {
249					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("target %s: %w", name, err)
250				}
251			}
252			// Fast-fail real targets at the request instead of letting them die
253			// mid-run inside NewRunner (which the browser only learns from a
254			// target_error event). demo:// targets need no repos or credential.
255			if !isDemoRemote(bt.Remote) {
256				if len(bt.Repos) == 0 {
257					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("target %s: no repos", name)
258				}
259				if bw.Strategy == "repo" && len(bt.Repos) < 2 {
260					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("target %s: strategy=repo needs >= 2 repos", name)
261				}
262				if ts.Secret == "" && ts.SecretSource == "" {
263					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("target %s: no credential (pass secret or secret_source)", name)
264				}
265			}
266			if bench.IsGitHubDotCom(bt.Remote) {
267				if hi := slices.Max(bw.Concurrency); hi > 16 {
268					warnings = append(warnings, fmt.Sprintf(
269						"concurrency %d against github.com is likely to trip secondary rate limits / abuse detection — keep it low (e.g. 1,4)", hi))
270				}
271			}
272			targets[i] = &targetState{id: i, name: name, spec: bt, col: &collector{}}
273		}
274	
275		// Reject a second concurrent start before doing any credential work:
276		// resolving a secret_source execs the operator's CLIs, which is wasted (and
277		// needlessly materializes tokens) for a request we're about to refuse. The
278		// authoritative check under m.mu below still guards the start/set race.
279		m.mu.Lock()
280		active := m.active != nil
281		m.mu.Unlock()
282		if active {
283			return nil, nil, errRunActive
284		}
285	
286		// Resolve CLI-sourced secrets concurrently: each exec can block on a slow
287		// CLI (15s timeout apiece), and serial resolution would stack that latency
288		// into this synchronous POST handler. Failures still surface here as a 400
289		// so a bad login is immediate feedback, not a mid-run target death.
290		var (
291			secWG   sync.WaitGroup
292			secMu   sync.Mutex
293			secErrs []error
294		)
295		for i, ts := range req.Targets {
296			if ts.SecretSource == "" {
297				continue
298			}
299			secWG.Add(1)
300			go func(t *targetState, source string) {
301				defer secWG.Done()
302				user, secret, err := resolveSecretSource(source, t.spec.Remote)
303				if err != nil {
304					secMu.Lock()
305					secErrs = append(secErrs, fmt.Errorf("target %s: %w", t.name, err))
306					secMu.Unlock()
307					return
308				}
309				t.spec.Secret = secret
310				if user != "" && t.spec.User == "" {
311					t.spec.User = user // e.g. glab → oauth2; explicit -user still wins
312				}
313			}(targets[i], ts.SecretSource)
314		}
315		secWG.Wait()
316		if len(secErrs) > 0 {
317			return nil, nil, errors.Join(secErrs...)
318		}
319	
320		ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
321		run := &Run{
322			ID: runID, StartedAt: time.Now(), log: newEventLog(),
323			ctx: ctx, cancel: cancel, done: make(chan struct{}),
324			workload: ws, bw: bw, state: "starting", targets: targets,
325		}
326	
327		m.mu.Lock()
328		if m.active != nil {
329			m.mu.Unlock()
330			cancel()
331			return nil, nil, errRunActive
332		}
333		m.active = run
334		m.runs[run.ID] = run
335		m.order = append(m.order, run.ID)
336		m.pruneLocked()
337		m.mu.Unlock()
338	
339		run.log.emit("hello", run.helloEvent())
340		go run.coordinate(m)
341		return run, warnings, nil
342	}

344	// pruneLocked drops the oldest finished runs beyond keepFinishedRuns.
345	// Caller holds m.mu.
346	func (m *RunManager) pruneLocked() {
347		finished := 0
348		for i := len(m.order) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
349			r := m.runs[m.order[i]]
350			if r == m.active {
351				continue
352			}
353			finished++
354			if finished > keepFinishedRuns {
355				delete(m.runs, m.order[i])
356				m.order = append(m.order[:i], m.order[i+1:]...)
357			}
358		}
359	}

369	// stopActive cancels the active run (if any) and waits for its coordinator to
370	// finish generating load, persist its results, and clean up — bounded by
371	// timeout so shutdown can't hang. Called on server shutdown so an embedded
372	// caller doesn't return while remote load continues and results are unwritten.
373	func (m *RunManager) stopActive(timeout time.Duration) {
374		m.mu.Lock()
375		run := m.active
376		m.mu.Unlock()
377		if run == nil {
378			return
379		}
380		run.cancel()
381		select {
382		case <-run.done:
383		case <-time.After(timeout):
384		}
385	}

387	// coordinate is the run's driver goroutine: build runners, then walk the
388	// concurrency sweep with a barrier per level so every target starts each
389	// level at the same instant (the whole point of a comparison run).
390	func (r *Run) coordinate(m *RunManager) {
391		defer close(r.done) // let a shutdown waiter know the run has fully finished
392		defer r.cancel()
393	
394		// Resolve every target concurrently — entiredb setup probes the cluster.
395		// A target that fails setup is dead but doesn't kill the comparison.
396		var wg sync.WaitGroup
397		for _, t := range r.targets {
398			wg.Add(1)
399			go func(t *targetState) {
400				defer wg.Done()
401				var (
402					lr  levelRunner
403					err error
404				)
405				if isDemoRemote(t.spec.Remote) {
406					lr, err = newDemoRunner(t.spec.Remote, r.bw, t.col)
407				} else {
408					lr, err = bench.NewRunner(r.ctx, t.spec, r.bw, t.col)
409				}
410				t.spec.Secret = "" // consumed; nothing on the run retains it
411				if err != nil {
412					r.markDead(t, -1, err)
413					return
414				}
415				r.mu.Lock()
416				t.runner = lr
417				t.label = lr.Label()
418				r.mu.Unlock()
419				r.log.emit("target_ready", map[string]any{
420					"target": t.id, "label": lr.Label(), "nodes": lr.Nodes(), "object_format": lr.ObjectFormat(),
421				})
422			}(t)
423		}
424		wg.Wait()
425	
426		if r.aliveTargets() == nil {
427			r.finish(m, "failed")
428			return
429		}
430		r.setState("running")
431	
432		// One ticker per run: a single bucket event per second carries every
433		// target's stats, so chart columns align by construction.
434		tickerDone := make(chan struct{})
435		tickerStopped := make(chan struct{})
436		go func() {
437			defer close(tickerStopped)
438			tick := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
439			defer tick.Stop()
440			for {
441				select {
442				case <-tick.C:
443					r.emitBucket()
444				case <-tickerDone:
445					return
446				}
447			}
448		}()
449	
450		for li, c := range r.bw.Concurrency {
451			if r.ctx.Err() != nil {
452				break
453			}
454			alive := r.aliveTargets()
455			if alive == nil {
456				break
457			}
458	
459			// Transition atomically under r.mu: reset every collector (fresh
460			// rolling window + warm-up boundary) and advance the level index
461			// together, so a bucket tick can never attribute the previous level's
462			// leftover samples to the new index. The prior level's agents have all
463			// returned (lwg.Wait below), so nothing races this reset.
464			r.mu.Lock()
465			for _, t := range alive {
466				t.col.reset(r.bw.Warmup)
467			}
468			r.levelIdx = li
469			r.levelConc = c
470			r.mu.Unlock()
471			r.log.emit("level_start", map[string]any{
472				"level_index": li, "concurrency": c,
473				"warmup_sec": r.bw.Warmup.Seconds(), "duration_sec": r.bw.Duration.Seconds(),
474				"at": time.Now().UTC(),
475			})
476	
477			// Real start barrier: every target builds its agents, then all are
478			// released together, so target-dependent setup time doesn't shift the
479			// measured windows.
480			barrier := bench.NewStartBarrier(len(alive))
481			var lwg sync.WaitGroup
482			for _, t := range alive {
483				lwg.Add(1)
484				go func(t *targetState) {
485					defer lwg.Done()
486					res, err := t.runner.RunLevel(r.ctx, c, barrier)
487					if err != nil {
488						r.markDead(t, li, err)
489						return
490					}
491					r.mu.Lock()
492					t.results = append(t.results, res)
493					r.mu.Unlock()
494				}(t)
495			}
496			barrier.Await() // all targets have built their agents (or failed and arrived)
497			barrier.Fire()  // release them to start the timed window together
498			lwg.Wait()
499	
500			// Flush the level's final partial second before the next level resets
501			// the collectors (or the run ends): the ticker only fires on whole
502			// seconds, so without this the tail — and every sample of a sub-second
503			// level — would be dropped from the live and persisted series even
504			// though the authoritative LevelResult counts it.
505			r.emitBucket()
506	
507			results := map[string]bench.LevelResult{}
508			r.mu.Lock()
509			for _, t := range r.targets {
510				if len(t.results) > li {
511					results[strconv.Itoa(t.id)] = t.results[li]
512				}
513			}
514			r.mu.Unlock()
515			r.log.emit("level_result", map[string]any{
516				"level_index": li, "concurrency": c, "targets": results,
517			})
518		}
519	
520		close(tickerDone)
521		<-tickerStopped
522	
523		state := "done"
524		if r.ctx.Err() != nil {
525			state = "cancelled"
526		} else if r.aliveTargets() == nil {
527			state = "failed"
528		}
529		r.finish(m, state)
530	}

545	// persistResults writes the run's format-2 result doc and returns its bare
546	// filename ("" on failure — the run still finishes; persistence is
547	// best-effort).
548	func (r *Run) persistResults(dir string) string {
549		r.mu.Lock()
550		doc := results.Doc{
551			Format:   2,
552			RunID:    r.ID,
553			Strategy: r.workload.Strategy,
554			Duration: r.bw.Duration.String(),
555			Warmup:   r.bw.Warmup.String(),
556			Commit:   r.bw.CommitDesc(),
557			State:    r.state,
558		}
559		for _, t := range r.targets {
560			doc.Targets = append(doc.Targets, results.TargetResult{
561				Name: t.name, Label: t.label, Error: t.fatalErr,
562				Levels: slices.Clone(t.results), Series: slices.Clone(t.series),
563			})
564		}
565		r.mu.Unlock()
566	
567		file := "forgemark-" + r.ID + ".json"
568		if err := results.Write(dir, file, doc); err != nil {
569			r.log.emit("target_error", map[string]any{
570				"target": -1, "level_index": -1, "fatal": false,
571				"message": "persist results: " + err.Error(),
572			})
573			return ""
574		}
575		return file
576	}

578	func (r *Run) emitBucket() {
579		now := time.Now().Unix()
580		// Hold r.mu across the whole tick so a level transition (which resets the
581		// collectors and advances levelIdx under the same lock) can't interleave:
582		// otherwise a snapshot could carry the previous level's samples under the
583		// new level index. The snapshot and series append are cheap and run once
584		// per second. Lock order is always r.mu → collector.mu, never reversed.
585		r.mu.Lock()
586		defer r.mu.Unlock()
587		li, c := r.levelIdx, r.levelConc
588		stats := make(map[string]BucketStats, len(r.targets))
589		for _, t := range r.targets {
590			if t.dead {
591				continue
592			}
593			st := t.col.snapshot()
594			stats[strconv.Itoa(t.id)] = st
595			if len(t.series) < maxBufferedEvents {
596				t.series = append(t.series, results.SeriesPoint{
597					T: now, Level: li, OK: st.OK, CAS: st.CAS, Err: st.Err,
598					P50: st.P50, P95: st.P95, P99: st.P99,
599					CloneOK: st.CloneOK, CloneErr: st.CloneErr,
600					CloneP50: st.CloneP50, CloneP95: st.CloneP95, CloneP99: st.CloneP99,
601				})
602			}
603		}
604		if len(stats) == 0 {
605			return
606		}
607		r.log.emit("bucket", map[string]any{
608			"level_index": li, "concurrency": c, "t": now, "targets": stats,
609		})
610	}

619		})

11	// windowSecs is the rolling-percentile window: latency percentiles in a bucket
12	// event are computed over the OK samples of the last windowSecs seconds, so a
13	// single quiet second doesn't blank the lines while spikes still show quickly.
14	const windowSecs = 10
15	
16	// collector is the live aggregator for one target of one run. It implements
17	// bench.Sink: agents call OnSample concurrently mid-measurement, so it does
18	// only counter increments and one append under its mutex. Once per second the
19	// run's ticker calls snapshot, which swaps the current bucket out and computes
20	// rolling percentiles (an exact sort over the window — a few thousand floats,
21	// ~100µs, nothing at benchmark sample rates).
22	type collector struct {
23		mu        sync.Mutex
24		warmup    time.Duration // samples before this offset are excluded (matches the level result)
25		cur       bucket
26		ring      [windowSecs][]float64 // push OK latencies, one slot per elapsed second
27		cloneRing [windowSecs][]float64
28		pos       int
29	}
30	
31	// bucket accumulates one second of samples.
32	type bucket struct {
33		ok, cas, errs     int
34		cloneOK, cloneErr int
35		lat               []float64 // OK push latencies (ms)
36		cloneLat          []float64 // OK clone latencies (ms)
37	}

39	// BucketStats is one target's slice of a per-second bucket event. Push and
40	// clone ops are reported separately, mirroring LevelResult; the UI picks the
41	// primary series from the workload strategy. Attempt totals are derivable
42	// (ok+cas+err, clone_ok+clone_err), so they aren't carried on the wire.
43	type BucketStats struct {
44		OK  int `json:"ok"`
45		CAS int `json:"cas"`
46		Err int `json:"err"`
47		// Rolling percentiles over the last windowSecs seconds of OK pushes.
48		P50 float64 `json:"p50_ms"`
49		P95 float64 `json:"p95_ms"`
50		P99 float64 `json:"p99_ms"`
51	
52		CloneOK  int     `json:"clone_ok,omitempty"`
53		CloneErr int     `json:"clone_err,omitempty"`
54		CloneP50 float64 `json:"clone_p50_ms,omitempty"`
55		CloneP95 float64 `json:"clone_p95_ms,omitempty"`
56		CloneP99 float64 `json:"clone_p99_ms,omitempty"`
57	}

59	func (c *collector) OnSample(s bench.Sample) {
60		ms := float64(s.Dur) / float64(time.Millisecond)
61		c.mu.Lock()
62		defer c.mu.Unlock()
63		// The Sink receives warm-up samples too; drop them so the live counts,
64		// rolling percentiles, and persisted series match the authoritative level
65		// result, which excludes the warm-up window.
66		if s.Offset < c.warmup {
67			return
68		}
69		if s.Op == bench.OpClone {
70			switch s.Res {
71			case bench.OutcomeOK:
72				c.cur.cloneOK++
73				c.cur.cloneLat = append(c.cur.cloneLat, ms)
74			default:
75				c.cur.cloneErr++
76			}
77			return
78		}
79		switch s.Res {
80		case bench.OutcomeOK:
81			c.cur.ok++
82			c.cur.lat = append(c.cur.lat, ms)
83		case bench.OutcomeCAS:
84			c.cur.cas++
85		default:
86			c.cur.errs++
87		}
88	}
89	
90	// snapshot closes out the current second: it returns its counters and the
91	// rolling percentiles over the updated window.
92	func (c *collector) snapshot() BucketStats {
93		c.mu.Lock()
94		b := c.cur
95		c.cur = bucket{}
96		c.ring[c.pos] = b.lat
97		c.cloneRing[c.pos] = b.cloneLat
98		c.pos = (c.pos + 1) % windowSecs
99		// Copy the ring's slice headers (cheap) and concatenate after unlocking:
100		// each window slot is a completed second's slice, never appended to in
101		// place, so holding the mutex across the O(window) concat would needlessly
102		// block concurrent OnSample calls and depress measured throughput.
103		ring, cloneRing := c.ring, c.cloneRing
104		c.mu.Unlock()
105	
106		var lat, cloneLat []float64
107		for i := range ring {
108			lat = append(lat, ring[i]...)
109			cloneLat = append(cloneLat, cloneRing[i]...)
110		}
111	
112		st := BucketStats{
113			OK: b.ok, CAS: b.cas, Err: b.errs,
114			CloneOK: b.cloneOK, CloneErr: b.cloneErr,
115		}
116		if len(lat) > 0 {
117			sort.Float64s(lat)
118			st.P50 = bench.Percentile(lat, 50)
119			st.P95 = bench.Percentile(lat, 95)
120			st.P99 = bench.Percentile(lat, 99)
121		}
122		if len(cloneLat) > 0 {
123			sort.Float64s(cloneLat)
124			st.CloneP50 = bench.Percentile(cloneLat, 50)
125			st.CloneP95 = bench.Percentile(cloneLat, 95)
126			st.CloneP99 = bench.Percentile(cloneLat, 99)
127		}
128		return st
129	}
130	
131	// reset clears the bucket and the rolling window and sets the warm-up boundary
132	// for the level about to start, so percentiles never bleed across concurrency
133	// levels and warm-up samples are excluded.
134	func (c *collector) reset(warmup time.Duration) {
135		c.mu.Lock()
136		defer c.mu.Unlock()
137		c.warmup = warmup
138		c.cur = bucket{}
139		c.ring = [windowSecs][]float64{}
140		c.cloneRing = [windowSecs][]float64{}
141		c.pos = 0
142	}

I have everything I need. Here's my honest triage before I touch anything, since not all 9 deserve the same treatment:

**Fixing (genuinely real):**
- **#1 server.go:92 (High)** — on a non-loopback bind we only refuse *pasted* secrets; a `secret_source` still makes the server spend the operator's gh/glab/entire credential on behalf of any reachable client. Closing it: non-loopback bind refuses *all* credential materialization (pasted or CLI-sourced), so only `demo://` runs work there. Also gating `/api/local/suggest` (it execs the CLIs and leaks the operator's handles/cluster).
- **#3 local.go:82 (High)** — audience check keeps only the hostname, so `http://github.com` passes and the token goes out over cleartext. Requiring `https` and rejecting userinfo for every CLI-sourced URL.
- **#2 compare-local.sh:106** — real shell-injection: `shlex.quote` output embedded *inside* a double-quoted `echo` gets re-evaluated. Trivial fix.
- **#5 newrun.js:225** — `NaN → null → silent default`. Validating numeric fields like concurrency already is.
- **#7 server.go:42** — read routes lack the rebinding Host guard. Cheap defense-in-depth.
- **#9 runmgr.go:474** — `level_start.at` is emitted before the barrier fires, so the UI countdown starts early by the setup time. Move it to fire time.
- **#8 server.go:68** — confirmed real: `deleteRef` cleanup runs on a detached 30s context, but shutdown only waits 10s, so the process can exit mid-cleanup and leak refs. Aligning the shutdown budget.

**Pushing back:**
- **#6 collector.go:61** — I don't buy it. `OnSample` holds the lock only for a counter bump + one slice append (sub-microsecond); git ops are tens-to-hundreds of ms. At 128 agents the contention is noise against operation latency, and `snapshot` already drops the lock before the O(window) concat. Sharding adds real complexity for immeasurable gain. Skipping unless you want it.
- **#4 runmgr.go:505** — real but cosmetic. It only affects the *live* sparkline's final partial-second point; the authoritative `LevelResult` throughput is computed over the true window and is unaffected. A full rate-normalization means a wire-format + UI + persisted-series change for a visual nit. I'll do the minimal honest thing (mark the flushed bucket partial so the UI can treat it differently) rather than the full refactor — tell me if you want the whole rate normalization.

Starting the fixes.

  a malformed entry no longer serializes to null and silently take a server
  default.

Both checks green. Pushed as `96f1d1e` on `feat/web-demo`.

## Round 4 verdict

Seven fixed, two I pushed back on. Ranked by what mattered:

**Fixed**
- **#1 (High) exposed-bind credential abuse** — the real teeth. A non-loopback bind now refuses *all* credential materialization (pasted and `secret_source`) and disables CLI discovery entirely. Exposed binds are demo-only; real-forge benchmarking requires the default loopback bind. I chose this over "add auth" deliberately: this is a local benchmark tool with no user model, and gating the credential path is the honest boundary, not bolting on a login system.
- **#3 (High) cleartext token** — `validateSecretAudience` now requires `https` and rejects userinfo on every CLI-sourced URL. `http://github.com` and `REDACTED` are both refused now.
- **#2 shell injection** — verified live: a crafted error with `$(touch …)` is now `shlex.quote`'d as one token and stays inert.
- **#7 rebinding on reads**, **#8 shutdown vs 30s cleanup**, **#9 `level_start` timing**, **#5 NaN→silent-default** — all done, with tests extended (https/userinfo cases, `secret_source` + suggest rejection on exposed bind, read-route rebinding).

**Declined / deferred**
- **#6 collector mutex** — declined. The lock covers a counter bump + one append against git ops that take tens-to-hundreds of ms; the perturbation is unmeasurable and `snapshot` already drops the lock before the O(window) concat. Sharding is complexity for nothing. Say the word if you disagree and I'll add it.
- **#4 fractional buckets** — real but cosmetic (live sparkline only; the authoritative `LevelResult` is computed over the true window and is correct). The proper fix is carrying per-bucket elapsed through the wire, the persisted `SeriesPoint`, and the UI. I didn't ship an inert `partial` flag. If you want the live chart exact, I'll do the full rate normalization as its own change — your call.

Still open from earlier: the no-op commit `bbf117a` is in the branch history. Want it dropped before merge?

The two build layers

  1. Definitions + a forgemark output adapter (small, mostly in this repo). The runners are JSON, but forgemark needs a machine-readable monitor mode: reduce a results.Doc to the runner's {"value": <n>,
  "rationale": "..."} last-JSON-line contract. A forgemark report --emit monitor (or a --format entire) over the existing engine + internal/results. Cheap, and it's the seam everything else hangs off.

  2. The runtime (the real work, needs Entire). Every stock runner uses the read-only claude sandbox. forgemark is different: it needs the forgemark binary, network egress to the target forge, and ideally
  regional placement (forgemark's whole methodology caveat is "run close to the target"). That's a new runner profile, and it's exactly where Entire's regional clusters + mirrors are the differentiator.
  Two ways to get the runtime.kind:
  - Reuse prompt_runner as an MVP: a runner whose prompt is "run forgemark ..., emit the result JSON as the last line" (works with today's adapter, if the sandbox allows egress).
  - A proper non-prompt kind. I saw hints of agent_runner, trail_runner, and one script_runner reference but no command_runner/exec_runner, so a measured/exec runner kind looks like a genuine gap
  forgemark would be the first real user of.

  Sequencing

  1. forgemark monitor-output mode — the adapter (this repo, no Entire dependency).
  2. CI/Gate proof — wire it into GitHub Actions on top of open PR #6's threshold flags: forgemark runs, emits the monitor value, gates the PR. Proves the signal with zero new Entire infra.
  3. Native Entire runner — the regional, egress-capable runtime that runs forgemark in-region and posts monitors to the Trail. The strategic headline.

  What I need from you

  1. Does a Gate already threshold a trail_monitor (so throughput < X fails a Trail), or is Gate still to build? That decides whether forgemark just emits and rides existing gating, or we build the gate
  too.
  2. Is there an exec/command/script_runner runtime, or would forgemark be the case that justifies one? This is the biggest scope fork.
  3. Sandbox reality: can a runner sandbox make outbound git connections and be pinned to a region? That's the gating constraint on the native runner.

  Want me to draft the four runner JSON files and the forgemark report --emit monitor adapter as a concrete first PR (layer 1), so there's something real to run in CI while the runtime questions get
  answered?

{"body":"## Summary\nforgemark can now gate CI runs: set `-min-push-rate`, `-max-p95`, or `-max-errors` and a sweep that misses any of them prints per-level breach lines to stderr and exits 2. All three flags default off; unset flags change nothing.\n\n## Why this matters\nThe results JSON is written \"for charting\" (README), but the process itself always exits 0 - `run()` returns `writeResults(...)` without inspecting the measured levels, so a deploy that halves push throughput still reads as a passing benchmark. Both reference tools in this space gate on results: [GitLab Performance Tool](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/support/workflows/gpt_quick_start/) ships built-in success thresholds on throughput and latency, and [k6](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/thresholds/) fails the process on a threshold breach. This adds the equivalent with three stdlib flags and a distinct exit code (0 ok, 1 operational error, 2 threshold breach), so a forge team can pin a floor on push/s and a ceiling on p95 in CI.\n\n## Demo\nSimulated demo:\n![demo](https://files.catbox.moe/abecxl.gif)\n\nVerified live against github.com: a c=1 run sustaining 1.0 push/s with `-min-push-rate 5 -max-p95 500ms` printed both breach lines and exited 2; the same run with `-min-push-rate 0.2 -max-p95 5s` exited 0 with `\"thresholds_ok\": true` in the JSON.\n\n## Changes\n- Threshold evaluation is a pure function over the existing `levelResult` fields (`checkThresholds` in stats.go), run after `writeResults` so the JSON is always written even when the run fails the gate.\n- Exit 2 is reserved for breaches via a sentinel error in `main()`, keeping it distinguishable from the hard-error exit 1 path.\n- The `thresholds` block (configured values plus breach list) only appears in the results JSON when at least one flag is set; unset runs produce byte-identical output.\n\n## Testing\nTable-driven `TestCheckThresholds` (breach / no-breach / unset), `TestParseFlagsThresholds`, and two `writeResults` JSON tests (thresholds present when configured, absent when unset). `go test ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt`, and `golangci-lint` all pass locally.\n","headRefName":"fix/forgemark-threshold-gate","state":"OPEN","title":"feat: add threshold flags for CI regression gating"}
